transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

No matter how interested I am, I can’t keep my attention on job training or applications long enough to finish them. It’s honestly embarrassing because I really want to work, but I just get stuck and can't seem to follow through on anything.
Did you have similar problems with inattention, restlessness, or being easily distracted as a child, before age 12?

Yes, these problems definitely go back to when I was a kid. Back in elementary school, my teachers were always moving my seat and sending notes home because I’d blurt out answers, wander around the classroom, and constantly lose my homework. I wasn't trying to misbehave, but I just couldn't seem to stay in one place or remember what I was supposed to be doing.
Do these attention and restlessness problems still happen in more than one setting, such as at home, school, work, or in relationships?

Yes, absolutely, it affects me in pretty much every part of my life. At home, I'm constantly pacing around, forgetting bills, and interrupting my family during talks, while at work I'd make careless mistakes on service tickets and get overwhelmed by paperwork. It’s the exact same pattern from my school days, just affecting my adult life now.
Do you also often feel very restless or act on impulse, like fidgeting, interrupting others, blurting things out, or having trouble waiting your turn?

Yes, absolutely. I'm constantly bouncing my legs or messing with my keys, and sitting still gives me this pent-up energy where I just have to get up and pace around. Waiting in lines drives me crazy, and I always catch myself cutting my family off and blurting things out before they can even finish.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview confirms a lifelong pattern of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity beginning in childhood before age 12, persisting into adulthood, occurring across multiple settings, and causing clear functional impairment in work and daily life. This is most consistent with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, predominantly inattentive/combined presentation coded here as F90.0.
